items.ms: $\sqrt{8^2 + (-2)^2$ $2\sqrt{17$ km h⁻¹ Uses trigonometry, e.g. $\tan-1\dfrac{2{8 = 14.0^\circ$ or $\tan-1\dfrac{8{2 = 76.0^\circ$ Correct method for the bearing: $90^\circ + 14.0^\circ$ or $180^\circ - 76.0^\circ$ 104° $\overrightarrow{SL = (12\mathbf{i + 3\mathbf{j) - (4\mathbf{i + 22\mathbf{j) = 8\mathbf{i - 19\mathbf{j$ Correct method for the bearing, e.g. $180^\circ - \tan-1\dfrac{8{19$ or $90^\circ + \tan-1\dfrac{19{8$ 157° $\mathbf{s = (4 + 8t)\mathbf{i + (22 - 2t)\mathbf{j$ $\overrightarrow{LS = \mathbf{s - (12\mathbf{i + 3\mathbf{j) = (8t - 8)\mathbf{i + (19 - 2t)\mathbf{j$ $d^2 = (8t - 8)^2 + (19 - 2t)^2$ $= 64t^2 - 128t + 64 + 361 - 76t + 4t^2 = 68t^2 - 204t + 425$ * $68t^2 - 204t + 425 = 17^2$ (or $\leqslant 289$) Solves their 3-term quadratic: $68t^2 - 204t + 136 = 0 \Rightarrow t^2 - 3t + 2 = 0$ $t = 1$ and $t = 2$ First visible at 9 am; visible for 1 hour
items.why: Jun 2026 Q7(b) asked how long a boat stays within 9 km of O, and Jun 2025 Q2(c) a bearing of one point from another; a lighthouse range combines the distance-squared quadratic with both kinds of bearing.

items.name: Forces treated as vectors. Resolution of forces
path: M1.5.1 - Forces treated as vectors. R
items.question: A light smooth pulley hangs from a fixed point $O$ on a horizontal ceiling by a light chain attached to the axle of the pulley. A light inextensible rope passes over the pulley. One end of the rope is attached to a bucket of mass 12 kg, which hangs with that part of the rope vertical. A builder holds the other end of the rope so that the part of the rope between the pulley and the builder is inclined at $40^\circ$ to the horizontal, as shown in the diagram. The bucket is modelled as a particle, and the rope and the chain lie in one vertical plane. The bucket is held at rest. Write down the tension in the rope. Find the magnitude of the resultant force exerted on the pulley by the rope. Find the size of the angle between the chain and the vertical. The builder now pulls the rope so that the bucket moves vertically upwards with constant acceleration 0.6 m s⁻². The part of the rope held by the builder remains inclined at $40^\circ$ to the horizontal. Find the magnitude of the force exerted on the pulley by the rope while the bucket is accelerating.
items.ms: $T = 12g = 117.6$ N Resolves the two tensions horizontally and vertically: horizontal component $12g\cos 40^\circ$, vertical component $12g + 12g\sin 40^\circ$ Horizontal component $90.1$ N and vertical component $193.2$ N (or exact equivalents) Uses Pythagoras: $R^2 = 90.09^2 + 193.19^2$ $R = 213$ N or 210 N The pulley is in equilibrium, so the chain acts along the line of the resultant in (b): $\tan\theta = \dfrac{12g\cos 40^\circ{12g + 12g\sin 40^\circ$ $\theta = 25^\circ$ Equation of motion for the bucket: $T - 12g = 12\times 0.6$ $T = 124.8$ N Force on the pulley $= 2\times 124.8\cos 25^\circ = 226$ N or 230 N
items.why: M1.5.1 has come up in 33 of 34 sessions, in 10 of its last 12 parts as the force a string exerts on a smooth pulley (last Jun 2026); a stationary pulley hung from a chain, whose direction must then be deduced, has not been asked.

items.question: A child sits on a swing. The child and the seat, of total mass 22 kg, are modelled as a particle $P$ and the ropes of the swing are modelled as a single light inextensible rope $OP$, where $O$ is a fixed point. A parent holds the child at rest with the rope taut and inclined at $25^\circ$ to the vertical, as shown in the diagram. The force exerted by the parent acts in the vertical plane containing $OP$. The parent first applies a horizontal force of magnitude $F$ newtons, as shown in the diagram. Find the tension in the rope, the value of $F$. The parent now holds the child at rest in the same position by applying the smallest possible force. Find the magnitude of this force and describe its direction.
items.ms: Resolves vertically: $T\cos 25^\circ = 22g$ $T = 238$ N or 240 N Resolves horizontally: $F = T\sin 25^\circ$ (or $F = 22g\tan 25^\circ$) $F = 101$ or 100 The force acts perpendicular to the rope $OP$, i.e. at $25^\circ$ above the horizontal, away from the vertical through $O$ Resolves perpendicular to $OP$: $F\min = 22g\sin 25^\circ$ $F\min = 91.1$ N or 91 N
items.why: M1.5.2 has come up in 33 of 34 sessions; a particle on a string held aside by a horizontal force is its simplest core set-up, and the least force needed (perpendicular to the string) does not appear among the recent questions.

items.name: Equilibrium of a particle under coplanar forces. Weight, normal…
path: M1.5.2 - Equilibrium of a particle un
items.question: A lamp of mass 15 kg hangs from the end $P$ of a light rod $AP$. The end $A$ of the rod is attached to a vertical wall. The lamp is also supported by a light wire $BP$, where $B$ is a point on the wall vertically above $A$. The rod is inclined at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal and the wire is inclined at $15^\circ$ to the horizontal, as shown in the diagram. The rod and the wire lie in a vertical plane perpendicular to the wall. The lamp is modelled as a particle at $P$, and the force exerted on $P$ by the rod acts along the rod. The system is in equilibrium. Find the tension in the wire. Find the magnitude of the force exerted on $P$ by the rod, and state whether the rod is in tension or in thrust. The wire will break if the tension in it exceeds 400 N. The lamp is replaced by a heavier lamp, and the angles are unchanged. Find the greatest mass of lamp that can be supported.
items.ms: Resolves horizontally: $S\cos 30^\circ = T\cos 15^\circ$ Resolves vertically: $S\sin 30^\circ + T\sin 15^\circ = 15g$ Both equations correct Solves to give $T = 180$ N Substitutes their $T$ into either equation, e.g. $S = \dfrac{T\cos 15^\circ{\cos 30^\circ$ $S = 201$ N or 200 N Thrust: the rod pushes $P$ away from $A$ (its force on $P$ has a horizontal component away from the wall, which balances the pull of the wire towards the wall) Uses $T$ proportional to the mass, or $\dfrac{mg\cos 30^\circ{\sin 45^\circ = 400$ $m = 33.3$ kg (or 33 kg)
items.why: The M1.5.2 spec names tension and thrust, but none of the recent past parts asks for the thrust in a light rod; loads held by strings at given angles (washing lines Oct 2025, Jun 2026) are the recurring core.

items.name: Equilibrium of a particle under coplanar forces. Weight, normal…
path: M1.5.2 - Equilibrium of a particle un
items.question: A light inextensible string has length 1.6 m. Its ends are attached to two fixed points $A$ and $B$ on a horizontal ceiling, where $AB = 1.2$ m. A small smooth ring $R$ of mass 0.4 kg is threaded on the string. A horizontal force of magnitude $P$ newtons is applied to $R$ so that $R$ hangs in equilibrium vertically below $B$, with both parts of the string taut, as shown in the diagram. The force acts in the vertical plane containing the string. Show that $BR = 0.35$ m. Find the tension in the string. Find the value of $P$. State how you have used the fact that the ring is smooth. The horizontal force is removed and $R$ comes to rest in equilibrium vertically below the midpoint of $AB$. Find the tension in the string in this position.
items.ms: Uses $AR = 1.6 - BR$ and Pythagoras in triangle $ABR$: $(1.6 - x)^2 = 1.2^2 + x^2$ $2.56 - 3.2x = 1.44$ $x = 0.35$ cso Uses $\sin\theta = \dfrac{0.35{1.25 = 0.28$ (or $\cos\theta = 0.96$), where $\theta$ is the angle $AR$ makes with the horizontal, and resolves vertically with the same tension $T$ in both parts $T + T\sin\theta = 0.4g$, i.e. $1.28T = 3.92$ $T = 3.06$ N or 3.1 N Resolves horizontally: $P = T\cos\theta$ $P = 2.94$ (exactly $0.3g$) The tension is the same in both parts of the string ($AR$ and $BR$) Each part of the string is 0.8 m long, so the angle $\phi$ each part makes with the horizontal has $\cos\phi = \dfrac{0.6{0.8$ Resolves vertically: $2T\sin\phi = 0.4g$ $T = 2.96$ N or 3.0 N
items.why: Strings carrying loads came up in Oct 2025 and Jun 2026; a smooth ring threaded on a string, where the equal tensions come from the model and the geometry must be found first, is a likely variation not asked recently.

items.name: Coefficient of friction
items.question: A decorator holds a small block of mass 1.5 kg at rest against a rough vertical wall by pushing it with a light pole. The pole is inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal and pushes upwards towards the wall, as shown in the diagram. The pole lies in a vertical plane perpendicular to the wall and the thrust in the pole has magnitude $P$ newtons. The coefficient of friction between the block and the wall is 0.5. The block is modelled as a particle. Given that the block is on the point of sliding down the wall, find the value of $P$. The decorator now holds the pole horizontal, still pushing the block towards the wall with a force of the same magnitude. Determine whether the block can remain at rest.
items.ms: Resolves horizontally, $R = P\cos 30^\circ$, and vertically, $P\sin 30^\circ + F = 1.5g$ Both equations correct Uses $F = 0.5R$ (friction acting up the wall): $P\sin 30^\circ + 0.5P\cos 30^\circ = 1.5g$ $P = 15.8$ Now $R = P$, so the maximum friction is $0.5\times 15.8 = 7.88$ N, compared with the weight $1.5g = 14.7$ N $7.88 < 14.7$, so friction cannot support the block: it slides down (cannot remain at rest)
items.why: Friction on a vertical surface was last asked in Oct 2023 (a ring on a rod); a block pressed against a wall by an inclined pole, whose push also helps to hold it up, is a fresh variant of the limiting-friction core.

items.name: Coefficient of friction
items.question: A small box of mass 2.5 kg is placed on a rough plank. One end of the plank is raised slowly so that the plank is inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The box stays at rest until $\theta = 26^\circ$, when it is on the point of sliding down the plank. The box is modelled as a particle and the coefficient of friction between the box and the plank is $\mu$. Show that $\mu = \tan 26^\circ$, and find the value of $\mu$ to 3 significant figures. A second box, of mass 5 kg, has the same coefficient of friction with the plank. The plank is again raised slowly from the horizontal. State, with a reason, the value of $\theta$ at which the second box is on the point of sliding.
items.ms: Resolves perpendicular to the plank: $R = 2.5g\cos 26^\circ$ Resolves parallel to the plank (friction up the plank): $F = 2.5g\sin 26^\circ$ Uses $F = \mu R$ because the box is on the point of sliding $\mu = \dfrac{2.5g\sin 26^\circ{2.5g\cos 26^\circ = \tan 26^\circ$ cso $\mu = 0.488$ $\theta = 26^\circ$ The mass cancels: the condition $\tan\theta = \mu$ does not depend on the mass of the box
items.why: M1.5.3 has come up in 30 of 34 sessions with limiting friction on an inclined plane at its core; the slipping condition $\mu = \tan\theta$ and its independence of the mass have not been asked directly in recent papers.

items.name: Coefficient of friction
items.question: A sledge of mass 12 kg is on a rough slope inclined at $24^\circ$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the sledge and the slope is 0.2. The sledge is held at rest by a light rope, which is inclined at $18^\circ$ to the line of greatest slope, as shown in the diagram. The rope and the line of greatest slope lie in the same vertical plane, and the tension in the rope is $T$ newtons. The sledge is modelled as a particle. Show that, if the rope were removed, the sledge would slide down the slope. Find the smallest value of $T$ for which the sledge remains at rest. Find the largest value of $T$ for which the sledge remains at rest. Given that $T = 60$, find the magnitude and direction of the frictional force acting on the sledge.
items.ms: Compares the component of the weight down the slope, $12g\sin 24^\circ = 47.8$ N, with the maximum friction $0.2\times 12g\cos 24^\circ = 21.5$ N $47.8 > 21.5$, so friction cannot hold the sledge and it slides cso Resolves perpendicular to the slope: $R + T\sin 18^\circ = 12g\cos 24^\circ$ $R = 107.43 - T\sin 18^\circ$ Resolves parallel to the slope with friction up the slope: $T\cos 18^\circ + F = 12g\sin 24^\circ$ Uses $F = 0.2R$ and solves: $T(\cos 18^\circ - 0.2\sin 18^\circ) = 12g(\sin 24^\circ - 0.2\cos 24^\circ)$ $T = 29.6$ Resolves parallel to the slope with friction down the slope: $T\cos 18^\circ = 12g\sin 24^\circ + F$, with $F = \mu R$ $T\cos 18^\circ = 47.83 + 0.2(107.43 - T\sin 18^\circ)$ $T = 68.4$ Resolves parallel to the slope: $60\cos 18^\circ = 12g\sin 24^\circ + F$ (or compares $57.06$ N with $47.83$ N) $F = 9.23$ N Friction acts down the slope, because $60\cos 18^\circ > 12g\sin 24^\circ$
items.why: Holding a particle on a rough inclined plane with an angled force recurs (Jan 2025, Jun 2025, Jun 2026); the whole range of the force was asked only once (ring on a rod, Oct 2023), and the direction of non-limiting friction is rarely tested.

items.name: Coefficient of friction
items.question: A small box $A$ of mass 4 kg rests on a rough horizontal table. Two light inextensible strings are attached to $A$. One string passes over a small smooth pulley $P$ fixed at one edge of the table and carries a particle $B$ of mass 3 kg, which hangs freely. The other string passes over a small smooth pulley $Q$ fixed at the opposite edge of the table and carries a particle $C$ of mass 1.5 kg, which hangs freely. The parts of the strings between $A$ and the pulleys are horizontal and lie in a vertical plane through $P$ and $Q$, as shown in the diagram. The box is modelled as a particle and the coefficient of friction between $A$ and the table is $\mu$. The system is in equilibrium with $A$ on the point of moving towards $P$. Write down the tension in each string. Show that $\mu = \dfrac{3{8$ A particle of mass $M$ kg is now attached to $C$, so that a particle of total mass $(1.5 + M)$ kg hangs from the string over $Q$. Find the greatest value of $M$ for which $A$ remains at rest. The extra particle is removed, so that $C$ again has mass 1.5 kg, and the system is again at rest with $A$ on the point of moving towards $P$. The string carrying $C$ is then cut, and $A$ starts to move towards $P$. Find the acceleration of $A$, the tension in the string attached to $B$.
items.ms: Tension in the string carrying $B$: $3g = 29.4$ N Tension in the string carrying $C$: $1.5g = 14.7$ N Resolves vertically for $A$: $R = 4g$ Resolves horizontally for $A$ with friction towards $Q$: $3g = 1.5g + F$ Uses $F = \mu R$ because $A$ is on the point of moving $1.5g = 4g\mu$, so $\mu = \dfrac{3{8$ cso For the greatest $M$, $A$ is on the point of moving towards $Q$, so friction now acts towards $P$ Resolves horizontally for $A$: $(1.5 + M)g = 3g + F$ Uses $F = \dfrac{3{8\times 4g$: $(1.5 + M)g = 3g + 1.5g$ $M = 3$ Equation of motion for $B$: $3g - T = 3a$, and for $A$ with $F = \mu R = 1.5g$: $T - 1.5g = 4a$ (or the whole system) Both equations correct $a = 2.1$ m s⁻² Substitutes their $a$ into the equation for $B$ or for $A$ $T = 23.1$ N
items.why: Limiting equilibrium of a particle joined by a string over a pulley recurs (Jan 2024, Jan 2026); a box held between two hanging loads, where the friction reverses direction as one load grows, has not been set.

items.name: Moments
items.question: A uniform plank $AB$, of length 5 m and mass 30 kg, rests in equilibrium in a horizontal position on two supports, one at $A$ and one at $C$, where $AC = 3.5$ m. A girl of mass 50 kg stands on the plank at the point $D$. The girl is modelled as a particle. The magnitude of the reaction on the plank at $C$ is three times the magnitude of the reaction on the plank at $A$. Find the magnitude of the reaction on the plank at $A$. Find the distance $AD$. State how you have used the fact that the plank is uniform.
items.ms: Resolving vertically: $R + 3R = 30g + 50g$ $R = 20g = 196$ N Moments about $A$ (or any other point), correct terms, dimensionally correct, e.g. $3R \times 3.5 = 30g \times 2.5 + 50g \times AD$ Correct equation with their $R$, e.g. $60g \times 3.5 = 75g + 50g \times AD$ $AD = 2.7$ m The weight of the plank acts at its midpoint (2.5 m from $A$)
items.why: Moments has been asked in 33 of 34 sessions; a plank on two supports with one reaction a multiple of the other recurs (Jun 2015 Q6, Jan 2017 Q4(b), Jan 2026 Q7), and the 'uniform' modelling mark was last asked in Jun 2023 Q4(c).

items.name: Moments
items.question: An angler holds a fishing rod $AB$ at rest in a horizontal position, as shown in the diagram. The rod has length 2.5 m and mass 0.8 kg and is modelled as a non-uniform rod with its centre of mass at $G$, where $AG = 0.75$ m. The angler holds the rod with one hand at $A$ and the other hand at $C$, where $AC = 0.5$ m. Each hand exerts a vertical force on the rod. A fish of mass 1.5 kg hangs from $B$ on a light vertical line. The fish is modelled as a particle. Find the magnitude of the force exerted on the rod by the hand at $C$. Find the magnitude of the force exerted on the rod by the hand at $A$ and state its direction. The angler can exert a force of at most 100 N with the hand at $A$. Keeping his hands at $A$ and $C$, he catches a larger fish, of mass $M$ kg, which hangs from $B$ instead. The rod is still at rest in a horizontal position. Find the greatest possible value of $M$.
items.ms: Moments about $A$, correct terms, dimensionally correct: $0.5F_C = 0.8g \times 0.75 + 1.5g \times 2.5$ Correct equation $F_C = 8.7g = 85.3$ N Resolving vertically, $F_A + 0.8g + 1.5g = F_C$, or moments about $C$: $0.5F_A = 0.8g \times 0.25 + 1.5g \times 2$ $F_A = 6.4g = 62.7$ N, vertically downwards Moments about $C$ with a force of 100 N at $A$: $100 \times 0.5 = 0.8g \times 0.25 + Mg \times 2$ $M = 2.45$
items.why: A fixed point that pushes down on a beam was last asked in Jun 2016 Q4 (diving board); a hand-held rod is a fresh context for the same idea, and a limit on one supporting force recurs (Jun 2016 Q4(b), Oct 2025 Q1(b)).

items.name: Moments
items.question: A uniform scaffold board $AB$ has length 3 m and weight 120 N. The board hangs in equilibrium in a horizontal position from two light vertical ropes, one attached to the board at $C$ and the other attached at $D$, where $AC = 0.4$ m and $DB = 0.6$ m. A tool box of weight 80 N is placed on the board at the point $P$, where $AP = x$ m, as shown in the diagram. The board is modelled as a rod and the tool box as a particle. Show that the tension in the rope at $D$ is $(50 + 40x)$ N. Find, in terms of $x$, the tension in the rope at $C$. Either rope will break if the tension in it exceeds 140 N. Find the range of possible values of $x$.
items.ms: Moments about $C$, correct terms, dimensionally correct: $2T_D = 120 \times 1.1 + 80(x - 0.4)$ Correct equation $T_D = 50 + 40x$ * Resolving vertically, $T_C + (50 + 40x) = 120 + 80$, or moments about $D$: $2T_C = 120 \times 0.9 + 80(2.4 - x)$ $T_C = (150 - 40x)$ N Uses $50 + 40x \le 140$ or $150 - 40x \le 140$ $x \le 2.25$ or $x \ge 0.25$ $0.25 \le x \le 2.25$
items.why: Tensions in terms of the position of a particle followed by a breaking-tension range came up in Jan 2016 Q5 and Oct 2025 Q1(b); with the ropes away from the ends both limits apply.

items.name: Moments
items.question: A non-uniform plank $AB$ has length 5 m and mass $M$ kg. The plank rests in a horizontal position on two supports at $C$ and $D$, where $AC = 1.5$ m and $DB = 1$ m, as shown in the diagram. The centre of mass of the plank is at $G$, where $AG = d$ m. The plank is modelled as a non-uniform rod and the boxes are modelled as particles. When a box of mass 8 kg is placed on the plank at $A$, and there is nothing else on the plank, the plank is on the point of tilting about $C$. Show that $M(d - 1.5) = 12$. The box at $A$ is removed and a box of mass 13 kg is placed on the plank at $B$. The plank is now on the point of tilting about $D$. Find the value of $M$ and the value of $d$. Both boxes are now placed on the plank at the same time, the 8 kg box at $A$ and the 13 kg box at $B$. Find the magnitude of the reaction on the plank at $C$.
items.ms: Reaction at $D$ is zero and moments about $C$: $8g \times 1.5 = Mg(d - 1.5)$ $M(d - 1.5) = 12$ * Reaction at $C$ is zero and moments about $D$: $13g \times 1 = Mg(4 - d)$ $M(4 - d) = 13$ Solves with (a), e.g. adding: $2.5M = 25$ $M = 10$ and $d = 2.7$ Moments about $D$, correct terms: $2.5R_C + 13g \times 1 = 8g \times 4 + 10g \times 1.3$ Correct equation (follow through their $M$ and $d$) $R_C = 12.8g = 125$ N
items.why: Two 'point of tilting' conditions giving two unknowns came up in Oct 2020 Q4, Jan 2021 Q4, Jan 2023 Q4 and Jun 2025 Q5; here the unknowns are the mass and the position of the centre of mass together.

items.name: Moments
items.question: A uniform plank $AB$, of length 4.4 m and mass 30 kg, rests in a horizontal position on two trestles at $C$ and $D$, where $AC = 1$ m and $DB = 1.4$ m, as shown in the diagram. A decorator of mass 75 kg stands on the plank at the point $P$. The plank is modelled as a uniform rod and the decorator as a particle. Given that $AP = 2.5$ m, find the magnitude of the reaction on the plank at $C$, at $D$. The decorator walks along the plank. Find the range of values of $AP$ for which the plank remains in equilibrium in a horizontal position. A block is placed on the plank at $A$ so that the decorator can stand at $B$ without the plank tilting. The block is modelled as a particle. Find the least possible mass of the block.
items.ms: Moments about $D$: $2R_C = 30g \times 0.8 + 75g \times 0.5$ $R_C = 30.75g = 301$ N Resolving vertically, $R_C + R_D = 105g$, or moments about $C$: $2R_D = 30g \times 1.2 + 75g \times 1.5$ $R_D = 74.25g = 728$ N Point of tilting about $C$, $R_D = 0$: $75g(1 - AP) = 30g \times 1.2$ $AP = 0.52$ m Point of tilting about $D$, $R_C = 0$: $75g(AP - 3) = 30g \times 0.8$ $AP = 3.32$ m $0.52 \le AP \le 3.32$ $R_C = 0$ and moments about $D$: $mg \times 3 + 30g \times 0.8 = 75g \times 1.4$ $m = 27$ kg
items.why: How far a person can walk before a plank tilts, and the least mass that prevents tilting, came up in Jun 2018 Q2(b), Jan 2019 Q4 and Jan 2022 Q3; here both tilting points are needed for the full range.

items.name: Moments
items.question: A steelyard is a simple weighing device. The diagram shows a steelyard made from a non-uniform rod $AB$ of length 0.96 m and mass 1.2 kg. The rod hangs from a fixed point by a light vertical string attached to the rod at $C$, where $AC = 0.12$ m. Goods are hung from a light hook at $A$. A small weight, the poise, of mass 0.4 kg can be hung from the rod at any point $P$ between $C$ and $B$, where $CP = x$ m. To weigh goods, the poise is moved until the rod rests in equilibrium in a horizontal position. The goods and the poise are modelled as particles. When nothing is hung from the hook, the rod rests horizontally in equilibrium when the poise is at the point $Z$, where $CZ = 0.09$ m. Find the distance of the centre of mass of the rod from $C$. Goods of mass $M$ kg are hung from the hook. Show that the rod rests horizontally in equilibrium when $x = 0.09 + 0.3M$. Given that $CB = 0.84$ m, find the greatest mass of goods that can be weighed with this steelyard. Find the tension in the string when the greatest mass of goods is being weighed. The poise is lost and is replaced by a poise of mass 0.3 kg. The marks on the rod still show the masses given by the equation in part (b). A bag of rice of mass 1.2 kg is weighed using the new poise. Find the mass that the steelyard shows for the bag of rice.
items.ms: Moments about $C$: $1.2g \times CG = 0.4g \times 0.09$ $CG = 0.03$ m Moments about $C$ with three terms: weight of goods, weight of rod and weight of poise $0.4g \times x = 1.2g \times 0.03 + Mg \times 0.12$ $x = 0.09 + 0.3M$ * $0.84 = 0.09 + 0.3M$ $M = 2.5$, so 2.5 kg Resolving vertically: $T = (1.2 + 0.4 + \text{their 2.5)g$ $T = 4.1g = 40.2$ N Moments about $C$ with the new poise: $0.3g \times x = 1.2g \times 0.03 + 1.2g \times 0.12$ $x = 0.6$ Substitutes their $x$ into $x = 0.09 + 0.3M$ 1.7 kg
items.why: Moments is asked in almost every session but always on planks, beams and ropes; a weighing device whose scale comes from a moments equation is the kind of unfamiliar context a late, long question could use.

items.name: Moments
items.question: A uniform beam $AB$, of length 5 m and mass 50 kg, rests in a horizontal position on two supports on a flat roof, one at $A$ and one at $C$, where $AC = 4$ m. The end $B$ projects beyond the edge of the roof. A small electric hoist of mass 5 kg is fixed to the beam at $B$. A crate of mass 50 kg hangs from the hoist by a light inextensible vertical cable, as shown in the diagram. The beam is modelled as a rod and the hoist and the crate are modelled as particles. The crate hangs at rest. Find the magnitude of the reaction on the beam at $A$ and the magnitude of the reaction on the beam at $C$. The hoist now raises the crate from rest. The crate moves vertically upwards with constant acceleration and rises 2.4 m in the first 4 s. Find the acceleration of the crate. Find the tension in the cable while the crate is accelerating. Find the magnitude of the reaction on the beam at $A$ while the crate is accelerating. Find the greatest acceleration with which the crate can be raised if the beam is to remain in equilibrium. State how you have used the fact that the cable is light.
items.ms: Moments about $C$: $4R_A + 55g \times 1 = 50g \times 1.5$ $R_A = 5g = 49$ N Resolving vertically, $R_A + R_C = 105g$, or moments about $A$: $4R_C = 50g \times 2.5 + 55g \times 5$ $R_C = 100g = 980$ N $s = ut + \tfrac{1{2at^2$ with $u = 0$: $2.4 = \tfrac{1{2a \times 4^2$ $a = 0.3$ m s⁻² Equation of motion for the crate: $T - 50g = 50 \times 0.3$ $T = 505$ N Moments about $C$ with a downward force of $5g + T$ at $B$: $4R_A + (5g + T) \times 1 = 50g \times 1.5$ $4R_A + 49 + 505 = 735$ $R_A = 45.25 = 45.3$ N Point of tilting about $C$, $R_A = 0$: $(5g + T) \times 1 = 50g \times 1.5$, so $T = 70g$ $70g - 50g = 50a$ $a = 0.4g = 3.92$ m s⁻² The tension is the same throughout the cable, so the downward force on the hoist equals the tension acting on the crate (the cable's weight is not included)
items.why: Every recent moments question (e.g. Jan 2026 Q4, Jun 2026 Q2) has its loads at rest; a beam carrying an accelerating load links moments with suvat and F = ma, and the 'light' modelling mark recurs (Jan 2022 Q7(d)).

items.name: The basic ideas of mathematical modelling as applied in…
path: M1.1.1 - The basic ideas of mathemati
items.question: A child slides from rest down a straight playground slide. The slide is 3.6 m long and is inclined at 35° to the horizontal, as shown in the diagram. The child is modelled as a particle and air resistance is ignored. Two models are used for the slide. Model A: the slide is smooth. Model B: the slide is rough and the coefficient of friction between the child and the slide is $\mu$. Using model A, find the time taken for the child to slide from the top to the bottom of the slide. In fact the child takes 1.6 s to slide from the top to the bottom of the slide. Using model B, find the value of $\mu$. State how you have used the modelling assumption that the child is a particle in your answer to part (b). Air resistance does in fact act on the child. Explain why, as a result, the value of $\mu$ found in part (b) is likely to be greater than the true value.
items.ms: Equation of motion down the slide: $mg\sin 35^\circ = ma \Rightarrow a = 9.8\sin 35^\circ = 5.62...$ $3.6 = \dfrac{1{2 \times 5.62... \times t^2$ $t = 1.1$ s (1.13 s) $3.6 = \dfrac{1{2a(1.6)^2 \Rightarrow a = 2.8125$ Resolving perpendicular to the slide: $R = mg\cos 35^\circ$ Equation of motion down the slide with $F = \mu R$: $mg\sin 35^\circ - \mu mg\cos 35^\circ = m \times 2.8125$ $\mu = 0.35$ The child's size is ignored, so the child moves exactly 3.6 m (the whole length of the slide); or all the forces act at a single point (so the child does not rotate) Air resistance also opposes the motion, so not all of the resistance to motion found in part (b) is friction So the frictional force is smaller than calculated and, as $R$ is unchanged, the true $\mu$ ($= F \div R$) is smaller
items.why: Modelling assumptions come up in about half the sessions as 1-mark 'state how the assumption was used' parts (Jun 2026 Q6(c), Jun 2023 Q4(c), Jan 2022 Q3(c)); comparing a smooth and a rough model, as Jun 2023 Q3 compared two students' models, gives the topic a whole question.

items.question: A café makes three types of sandwich each day: vegan, chicken and tuna. Each day it makes $x$ vegan sandwiches, $y$ chicken sandwiches and $z$ tuna sandwiches. The owner requires that at least 30% of the sandwiches made each day are vegan. Write this as an inequality in $x$, $y$ and $z$, with integer coefficients, in its simplest form. The owner also requires that there are at least 2 chicken sandwiches for every 3 vegan sandwiches. Lena writes this constraint as $2y \geqslant 3x$. Explain why Lena's constraint is incorrect and write down the correct constraint.

items.question: A call centre must have exactly 40 staff working on each shift. The staff are full-time, part-time or temporary. • Each full-time member of staff costs £120 per shift and can handle 60 calls. • Each part-time member of staff costs £80 per shift and can handle 45 calls. • Each temporary member of staff costs £100 per shift and can handle 40 calls. The staff on a shift must be able to handle at least 2000 calls. At least 25% of the staff on a shift must be full-time and there can be no more than 10 temporary staff on a shift. The manager wants to minimise the cost of the staff on each shift. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the numbers of full-time, part-time and temporary staff on a shift. Formulate this as a linear programming problem in $x$, $y$ and $z$, stating the objective and listing the constraints as simplified equations or inequalities with integer coefficients. Use the equation in your answer to part (a) to show that the objective is equivalent to $$\text{Minimise Q = 2x + z$$ Hence write the calls constraint, and the condition that the number of part-time staff cannot be negative, as simplified inequalities in $x$ and $z$ only.
items.ms: Minimise $C = 120x + 80y + 100z$ (or $6x + 4y + 5z$) $x + y + z = 40$ and $12x + 9y + 8z \geqslant 400$ $x \geqslant 10$ (or $3x \geqslant y + z$), $z \leqslant 10$ and $x, y, z \geqslant 0$ Substitutes $y = 40 - x - z$ into $C$ $C = 3200 + 40x + 20z$ $C = 3200 + 20(2x + z)$: 3200 is a constant and $20 > 0$, so minimising $C$ is equivalent to minimising $Q = 2x + z$ $3x - z \geqslant 40$ (from $60x + 45(40 - x - z) + 40z \geqslant 2000$) $x + z \leqslant 40$ (from $y = 40 - x - z \geqslant 0$)
items.why: Jun 2026 Q8(a) asked for a three-variable objective to be rewritten in two variables using an equality; a minimisation with an equality constraint is the less-practised variant.

items.question: A bakery makes $x$ trays of bread rolls and $y$ trays of pastries each day. The graph shows the constraints on its daily production. The profit on a tray of bread rolls is £40 and the profit on a tray of pastries is £50. Use the vertex method to find the number of trays of each type that the bakery should make each day to maximise its profit. State the maximum profit. Write down the objective, in terms of $x$, $y$ and $z$. Show that the problem becomes Maximise $4x + 5y$ subject to $$2x + 3y \leqslant 440, \quad x + y \leqslant 180, \quad 3x - 2y \geqslant 80, \quad 3y \geqslant x, \quad x, y \geqslant 0$$ The line $3y = x$ has been drawn on the grid below. items.question: A workshop makes garden benches and picnic tables. Each week it makes $x$ benches and $y$ tables. • Each bench needs 3 hours of carpentry and 2 hours of finishing. • Each table needs 5 hours of carpentry and 1 hour of finishing. • Each week 130 hours of carpentry and 48 hours of finishing are available. • At least 30% of the items made each week must be benches. • At least 5 tables must be made each week. The profit on each bench is £70 and the profit on each table is £110. The workshop wishes to maximise its weekly profit. Formulate this as a linear programming problem in $x$ and $y$, stating the objective and listing the constraints as simplified inequalities with integer coefficients. Represent your constraints on the grid below. Hence determine the feasible region and label it R. Use the vertex method to find the exact coordinates of the optimal vertex of R. The workshop can only make whole numbers of benches and tables. Determine the number of benches and the number of tables that the workshop should make each week, and the maximum weekly profit. For your answer to part (d), find the number of hours of carpentry and the number of hours of finishing that are unused each week.
items.ms: Maximise $P = 70x + 110y$ (or $7x + 11y$) Attempts both time constraints, e.g. $3x + 5y \ldots 130$ and $2x + y \ldots 48$ $3x + 5y \leqslant 130$ and $2x + y \leqslant 48$ $x \ldots 0.3(x + y)$ oe $7x \geqslant 3y$ $y \geqslant 5$ and $x \geqslant 0$ Two lines drawn correctly All four lines drawn correctly: $3x + 5y = 130$ through $(0, 26)$ and $(10, 20)$, $2x + y = 48$ through $(0, 48)$ and $(24, 0)$, $7x = 3y$ through $(0, 0)$ and $(15, 35)$, $y = 5$ R correctly identified and labelled Attempts to solve at least three pairs of equations simultaneously to find vertices of R Two vertices and their profits correct All four vertices and profits correct: $\left(\dfrac{15{7, 5\right)$: £700.00; $\left(\dfrac{43{2, 5\right)$: £2055.00; $\left(\dfrac{110{7, \dfrac{116{7\right)$: £2922.86; $\left(\dfrac{195{22, \dfrac{455{22\right)$: £2895.45 Optimal vertex $\left(\dfrac{110{7, \dfrac{116{7\right)$ Considers at least three integer points near the optimal vertex, checking that they are in R and finding their profits, e.g. $(15, 16)$: £2810, $(16, 16)$: £2880, $(14, 17)$: £2850, $(15, 17)$: £2920 $(15, 17)$ identified as optimal 15 benches and 17 tables; maximum profit £2920 Carpentry: $3(15) + 5(17) = 130$, so 0 hours unused Finishing: $2(15) + 17 = 47$, so 1 hour unused
items.why: Long LP questions (Jan 2026 Q8, Jun 2025 Q5) combine formulation, a graph, the vertex method and an integer solution; here two close vertices make the vertex method essential.

items.question: A restaurant is being opened. The activities involved, and the order in which they must be done, are described below. • Signing the lease (A), recruiting the staff (B) and designing the menu (C) can all start at the beginning of the project. • The kitchen can be refitted (D) and the seating area decorated (E) once the lease has been signed. • The extraction system can be fitted (F) once the kitchen has been refitted. • Staff training (G) takes place in the refitted kitchen, so it can start only when the staff have been recruited and the kitchen has been refitted. • Once the menu has been designed, the menus can be printed (H), the till can be programmed with the prices (I) and the advertising can begin (K). • The trial opening day (J) can take place only when every other activity, except the advertising, has been completed. • The project is complete when the trial opening day and the advertising have both been completed. Complete the precedence table, giving only the immediately preceding activities for each activity. Draw the activity network for this project, using activity on arc and the minimum number of dummies. Dummies are used in activity networks for two different reasons. Explain each reason, referring to activities in this project.
items.ms: D: A, E: A and F: D G: B, D and H: C, I: C, K: C J: E, F, G, H, I only At least six activities, one start and at least one dummy placed A, B, C, D, E and F placed correctly G and the first dummy placed correctly (a dummy from the end of D to the start of G, as G follows B and D but F follows D only) All eleven activities used, one finish H, I, J, K and the second dummy placed correctly (H and I both follow C and both precede only J), arrows on all activities and dummies, exactly two dummies To show dependence correctly: G depends on B and D but F depends on D only, so a dummy from the end of D lets G wait for D without F having to wait for B To keep activities uniquely defined: H and I start at the same event (after C) and both must finish before J, so a dummy is needed so that H and I do not have the same start and end events
items.why: Network drawing is hot (13 of 16 sessions) but the precedence table has always been given; building it from a written description, keeping only immediate predecessors, is the likeliest surprise, and the purpose of a dummy was asked in Jan 2025 Q7(a).

items.question: The network shows the activities needed to complete a project. Each activity is represented by an arc and its duration, in days, is shown in brackets. The early event times and late event times are shown at each vertex. Explain why the late event time for event 5 is 17. State the critical activities. Complete the table to show the earliest start time, earliest finish time, latest start time and latest finish time of each activity. Activity P starts at a critical event and ends at a critical event. Explain why P is not a critical activity. The start of activity J is delayed by 8 days. Determine the effect of this delay on the minimum completion time of the project. You must give a reason.
items.ms: Considers both arcs leaving event 5: the dummy gives 22 − 0 = 22 and J gives 22 − 5 = 17 The late event time is the smaller of these values, so 17 (J must start by day 17 or M and the project are delayed) A, C, G, K, N Earliest start times 6, 4, 12, 11 Earliest finish times 9, 11, 21, 16 Latest start times 10, 10, 13, 17 Latest finish times 13, 17, 22, 22 The time available for P is 24 − 11 = 13 days (both events have equal early and late times) P lasts only 8 days, so its total float is 13 − 8 = 5 > 0: P can be delayed without delaying the project Total float of J = 22 − 11 − 5 = 6 days (or J can start as late as day 17) 8 > 6, so the project is delayed by 2 days: completion time 30 days
items.why: Event times are asked every session, but recent parts are almost all 'complete the diagram'; the spec also names the algorithm and earliest/latest start and finish times of activities, which are the likeliest new angles, and a delayed start was asked in Jun 2026 Q7(f).

items.question: The shuttle sort is an algorithm that sorts a list of $n$ numbers into ascending order. It is carried out in passes, as follows. • In pass $k$, for $k = 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1$, the $(k + 1)$th number in the list is compared with the number immediately to its left. If it is smaller, the two numbers are swapped and the moved number is then compared with the next number to its left. This continues until the moved number is not smaller than the number to its left, or it reaches the start of the list. • After pass $n - 1$ the list is in ascending order. The list below is to be sorted into ascending order. $$32\quad 22\quad 26\quad 11\quad 43\quad 13\quad 57$$ Carry out the shuttle sort. Complete the table to show the list after each pass, and the number of comparisons and the number of swaps made in each pass. The original list is now sorted into ascending order using a bubble sort, starting at the left-hand end of the list. Each pass makes one fewer comparison than the pass before, and the sort stops after a pass in which no swaps are made. Showing the state of the list after each pass, find the total number of comparisons and the total number of swaps made by the bubble sort. Use your answers to parts (a) and (b) to compare the two algorithms when they are used to sort this list.
items.ms: Shuttle sort applied: lists after passes 1 and 2 correct Lists after all six passes correct Comparisons correct: 1, 2, 3, 1, 5, 1 Swaps correct: 1, 1, 3, 0, 4, 0 Bubble sort with the first two passes correct 20 comparisons 9 swaps The shuttle sort made fewer comparisons (13 compared with 20), so it was more efficient for this list Both algorithms made the same number of swaps (9)
items.why: Comparison and swap counts for a bubble sort were asked in Jan2021 Q3(b) and Jan2023 Q3(b); an unfamiliar sort given in words (D1.1.1) and compared with the bubble sort is a likely way to join the two spec points.

items.question: A gym has 13 members. Their membership numbers are $$350\quad 266\quad 153\quad 382\quad 361\quad 333\quad 291\quad 201\quad 183\quad 133\quad 319\quad 282\quad 392$$ Use a quick sort to obtain the list of membership numbers in ascending order. You should show the result of each pass and identify your pivots clearly. Use the binary search algorithm on your sorted list to locate the membership number 266. You must make your choice of pivots clear and state which part of the list is rejected at each stage. The gym plans to keep a sorted list of 2500 membership numbers. Find the maximum number of iterations of the binary search algorithm that could be needed to locate a membership number in this list. An interpolation search is an alternative to the binary search. For a list $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ in ascending order and a target value $T$, it uses the following algorithm, where $\mathrm{INT(y)$ means the integer part of $y$. Step 1 Let $L = 1$ and $U = n$ Step 2 If $T < x_L$ or $T > x_U$, output 'not in list' and stop Step 3 If $L = U$, let $P = L$. Otherwise let $P = L + \mathrm{INT\left(\dfrac{(T - x_L)(U - L){x_U - x_L\right)$ Step 4 If $x_P = T$, output $P$ and stop Step 5 If $x_P < T$, let $L = P + 1$. If $x_P > T$, let $U = P - 1$ Step 6 Go to Step 2 Apply the interpolation search to your sorted list to locate the membership number 266. Complete the table, giving the values each time Step 3 is used, and state the output. You may not need to use all the rows of the table. Compare the number of membership numbers examined by the two searches. Give one reason why the interpolation search could need to examine more numbers than the binary search when it is used on a different list.
items.ms: Quick sort with the middle item as pivot (291); after the first pass the list reads (values less than the pivot), pivot, (values greater than the pivot) First two passes correct and the next pivots chosen correctly Third pass correct, following through from their second pass and choice of pivots Fully correct sort, with the sort shown to be complete Middle-right pivot: position 7 (291), rejecting positions 7 to 13 Second and third pivots correct: 201 (position 4) and 282 (position 6), each correctly rejected Fourth pivot: position 5, 266 found $211 = 2048 \leq 2500 < 4096 = 212$ oe, or repeated halving of 2500 12 iterations Correct first use of Step 3: $P = 1 + \mathrm{INT\left(\dfrac{(266 - 133)(13 - 1){392 - 133\right) = 1 + \mathrm{INT(6.16)$ $P = 7$, $x_P = 291$, so $U = 6$ Second use of Step 3 with $L = 1$, $U = 6$: $P = 1 + \mathrm{INT\left(\dfrac{(266 - 133)(6 - 1){282 - 133\right) = 1 + \mathrm{INT(4.46)$ $P = 5$, $x_P = 266$, output 5 The interpolation search examined 2 numbers (291 and 266); the binary search examined 4 If the values in a list are unevenly spread (e.g. bunched together, or one value much larger than the rest), the estimated position $P$ can be far from the target, so many numbers (possibly one at a time) may be examined
items.why: Binary search has appeared in 5 of 16 sessions (Jan2021 to Jan2026) and quick sort in most; an unfamiliar search algorithm given in text (D1.1.1) to set against the binary search has never been set and is the likeliest synoptic surprise.

items.question: The diagram shows the aisles in a warehouse. The number on each arc is the length, in metres, of the aisle. The total length of the aisles is 268 m. A stock checker needs to walk along every aisle. State, with a reason, whether the network is Eulerian, semi-Eulerian or neither. The stock checker must start and finish at the office, A. Use the route inspection algorithm to find the length of the shortest inspection route. You should make your method and working clear, considering all possible pairings of the odd vertices, and state the aisles that must be walked twice. The stock checker now decides to start at one vertex and finish at a different vertex, so that the route is as short as possible. Every aisle must still be walked at least once. State the two vertices at which the stock checker should start and finish, and find the length of the route.
items.ms: Neither, as there are four vertices of odd degree (B, C, E and F) Three distinct pairings of the four odd vertices B, C, E and F considered Two rows correct: BC + EF = 45 + 32 = 77, BE + CF = 34 + 34 = 68, BF + CE = 59 + 35 = 94 All three rows correct and BE + CF = 68 chosen: aisles BD, DE and CF walked twice Length 268 + 68 = 336 m Selects the smallest of the six odd-vertex distances, EF = 32 (via G), to be repeated, so the route goes between the other two odd vertices B and C Start at B and finish at C (or start at C and finish at B); length 268 + 32 = 300 m
items.why: Route inspection has come up in 16 of 16 sessions; classifying the network and the closed route with all pairings were both on Jan 2026 and Jun 2026, and choosing the start and finish to shorten the route recurs.

items.question: A security guard patrols the corridors of a museum. The matrix shows the lengths, in metres, of the corridors that directly connect six galleries, A, B, C, D, E and F. A dash (–) shows that there is no corridor directly connecting two galleries. The total length of the corridors is 212 m. Draw the network represented by the matrix on the diagram below. Explain, with reference to the matrix, why the network is not Eulerian. The guard must walk along every corridor at least once, starting and finishing at A. Use the route inspection algorithm to find the length of the guard's shortest route. You must make your method clear, consider all possible pairings and state the corridors that must be walked twice. State the number of times that the guard's route in (c) passes through gallery C. Give a reason for your answer.
items.ms: At least eight of the ten arcs drawn between the correct vertices All ten arcs (AB, AC, AE, BC, BD, BF, CD, CE, DF, EF) correct with their weights, and no extra arcs Rows A, D, E and F each contain three entries, so these vertices have odd degree; an Eulerian network needs every vertex to have even degree Three distinct pairings of the odd vertices A, D, E and F considered Two rows correct: AD + EF = 27 + 15 = 42, AE + DF = 24 + 25 = 49, AF + DE = 39 + 35 = 74 All three rows correct and AD + EF = 42 chosen: corridors AC, CD and EF walked twice Length 212 + 42 = 254 m C has degree 4 and both repeated corridors AC and CD end at C, so in the route C has degree 6 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so the route passes through C three times
items.why: Route inspection has come up in 16 of 16 sessions; the D1.2.1 guidance says networks may be given as a matrix, which has not been combined with route inspection, and counting visits to a vertex is a rarely asked follow-up.

items.question: The diagram shows the overhead power lines between eight electricity substations, A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H. The number on each arc is the length, in km, of the power line. The total length of the power lines is 302 km. An engineer must inspect every power line. Explain why, in any network, the number of vertices of odd degree must be even. The engineer must start and finish at A. Use the route inspection algorithm to find the length of the engineer's shortest route. State the power lines that must be inspected twice. You must make your method clear and consider all possible pairings. The engineer now starts at C and must finish at H. Find the length of the shortest route that inspects every power line. You must make your method clear. A new power line of length 15 km is to be built directly between D and G. It must also be inspected. Determine whether building this power line would increase or decrease the length of the engineer's shortest route that starts and finishes at A.
items.ms: Each arc has two ends, so it adds 2 to the sum of the degrees: the sum of the degrees is even (twice the number of arcs) The even vertices contribute an even total, so the odd vertices must also give an even total, which needs an even number of odd vertices Three distinct pairings of the odd vertices C, D, F and G considered Two rows correct: CD + FG = 36 + 36 = 72, CF + DG = 50 + 45 = 95, CG + DF = 65 + 14 = 79 All three rows correct and CD + FG = 72 chosen: power lines BC, BD and FG inspected twice Length 302 + 72 = 374 km Recognises that D, F, G and H are the vertices to be paired (C is the start, and H, which has even degree, becomes an end of the route) DF + GH = 14 + 33 = 47, DG + FH = 45 + 13 = 58, DH + FG = 27 + 36 = 63 DF + GH chosen; length 302 + 47 = 349 km D and G become even, so only C and F are odd; repeat CF = 50 (C–B–D–F), giving 302 + 15 + 50 = 367 367 < 374, so the length of the route decreases (by 7 km)
items.why: Route inspection has come up in 16 of 16 sessions; a start and finish at given vertices was asked in Jan 2026, but a finishing vertex of even degree, the handshaking argument and the effect of adding an arc have not been asked.

items.question: The diagram shows the walkways between eight buildings, A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H, on a university campus. The number on each arc is the length, in metres, of the walkway. The lengths of four of the walkways are given in terms of $x$. The total length of the walkways is $(6x + 189)$ m. A security officer must walk along every walkway at least once, starting and finishing at A. Explain why A C D B C E is a walk in the network but is not a path. Given that the shortest route for the security officer repeats the walkways BC, CD and FG, find the range of possible values of $x$. You must make your method and working clear. Given instead that the length of the security officer's shortest route is 320 m, find the value of $x$. You must justify your answer. Using your value of $x$ from (c), write down a possible route of minimum length for the security officer, starting and finishing at A, and state its length.
items.ms: Each pair of consecutive vertices is joined by an arc of the network (AC, CD, DB, BC, CE), so the end vertex of each arc is the start vertex of the next: it is a walk Vertex C appears twice, so it is not a path (no vertex may appear more than once in a path) Odd vertices B, D, F and G identified and the three pairings BD + FG, BF + DG, BG + DF considered Forms an inequality for B to D via C being shorter than the direct walkway: $(x + 6) + (x + 10) < 3x + 2$ $x > 14$ Forms an inequality for the direct walkway FG being shorter than F–H–G: $x + 9 < 15 + 19$ $x < 25$, so $14 < x < 25$ Uses the total length $6x + 189$ with a pairing expression, e.g. for $14 < x < 25$: $6x + 189 + 3x + 25 = 320$ gives $x = 11.8$, which is not in this range Recognises that for $x < 14$ the walkways BD and FG are repeated: extra length $(3x + 2) + (x + 9)$ $6x + 189 + 4x + 11 = 320$, i.e. $10x + 200 = 320$ $x = 12$, which satisfies $x < 14$ (BD $= 38 < 40 =$ BC + CD and FG $= 21 < 34$) A closed route from A of 13 arcs (14 vertices) that repeats BD and FG A correct route, e.g. A B D B C D F G F H G E C A Length 320 m
items.why: Route inspection has come up in 16 of 16 sessions; Jun 2026 Q8 put arcs in terms of x and asked for the range of x and whether a walk is a path, so algebraic weights are likely again; finding x from a given route length, where the repeated arcs change, has not been asked.

items.question: A courier must visit six depots, A, B, C, D, E and F, starting and finishing at depot A. Every pair of depots is joined by a direct road. The table shows the journey time, in minutes, along the direct road between each pair of depots. Explain the difference between the classical and the practical travelling salesperson problems. By considering depots C, D and F, explain why the journey times in the table do not satisfy the triangle inequality. Write down the value that should replace the time for DF in a table of least journey times. Using the table with your amended value, apply the nearest neighbour algorithm, starting at A, to find an upper bound for the courier's journey time. State your route. Interpret the route found in (d) in terms of the depots that the courier actually passes through.
items.ms: Classical problem: each vertex must be visited exactly once before returning to the start Practical problem: each vertex must be visited at least once before returning to the start Compares the direct time DF = 53 with the time via C: DC + CF = 33 + 14 = 47 47 < 53, so the direct road is not the quickest way from D to F: one side of triangle CDF is longer than the sum of the other two, so the triangle inequality is not satisfied 47 (minutes) Nearest neighbour from A attempted: first four vertices A, E, C, F correct (arcs AE, EC, CF) Route A E C F D B A Upper bound 171 minutes The leg from F to D is driven via C (F to C to D, 14 + 33 = 47 minutes) A E C F C D B A (total time still 171 minutes)
items.why: Classical versus practical travelling salesperson is overdue (last asked Jan 2025); the spec's 'complete graphs satisfying the triangle inequality' has not been tested directly, and interpreting a route in the real network was asked in Jun 2021 and Jun 2022.

State the route that you use and its length.

items.question: Raj is an engineer. He must service seven wind turbines, A, B, C, D, E, F and G, starting and finishing at turbine A. The table shows the shortest distances, in km, between the turbines. By deleting C and all of its arcs, find a lower bound for the length of Raj's route. By deleting A and all of its arcs, find a second lower bound for the length of Raj's route. State which of your two lower bounds is the better lower bound, giving a reason. The nearest neighbour route starting at A has length 182 km. Write down the smallest interval that must contain the length of Raj's optimal route. Raj's colleague claims that she has found a route of length 158 km that visits every turbine and returns to A. Explain why her claim cannot be correct. Explain why the method used in (a) always gives a value that is no greater than the length of the optimal route.
items.ms: Residual minimum spanning tree found: arcs DF, BG, DG, AE, AF, weight 97 Adds the two shortest arcs from C: 31 + 33 Lower bound 161 km Residual minimum spanning tree of weight 104 (BG, DG, DF, CF, CE) plus the two shortest arcs from A (20 + 31) Lower bound 155 km 161 km, because it is the larger (higher) of the two lower bounds 161 ≤ length ≤ 182 158 is less than the lower bound of 161 km, and no route can be shorter than a lower bound (it does not matter that 158 > 155) Removing the deleted vertex and its two arcs from any route leaves a path through all the other vertices; this path is a spanning tree of them, so its length is at least that of the residual minimum spanning tree The route uses exactly two arcs at the deleted vertex, and these are at least as long as the two shortest arcs from it, so the route ≥ residual tree + two shortest arcs
items.why: Lower bounds by deleting a vertex and the smallest interval have been asked in 16 of 16 sessions (Jun 2026 Q4 and Q7); justifying the method and using the better bound to reject a claimed route have not been asked.

A sales representative must visit every town, starting and finishing at A. The incomplete table shows the shortest distances, in km, between the towns. Find the three missing values in the table. items.ms: AD = 26 (A–B–D) AG = 54 (A–C–F–G) CE = 60 (C–F–G–E) First three arcs AC, AB, BD chosen in order (or first four vertices A, C, B, D) First five arcs AC, AB, BD, CF, FG in order All six arcs AC, AB, BD, CF, FG, EG in order (weight 99 km) 2 × 99 = 198 km Residual minimum spanning tree of weight 80 (AC, AB, BD, CF, FG) Adds the two shortest arcs from E: EG + ED = 19 + 38 Lower bound 137 km The residual tree is a single path D–B–A–C–F–G whose two ends, D and G, are the vertices joined to E by the two shortest arcs So the arcs form a cycle through every town once: A B D E G F C A (or the reverse), of length 137 km A route of length 137 km exists and no route can be shorter than the lower bound of 137 km, so 137 km is optimal (lower bound = upper bound)
items.why: Bounds from minimum spanning trees are asked in every session; the spec guidance includes converting a network into a table of shortest distances, and a lower bound that is itself a tour (proving optimality) is a likely unseen angle.

items.ms: Nearest neighbour started at A: AF (15) chosen first, then the tie at F between FB and FD (both 23) recognised, with the first three vertices of either route correct (AFB… or AFD…) One route correct: A F B C E D A Second route correct: A F D E B C A Both lengths correct: AFBCEDA = 139 km and AFDEBCA = 117 km AFDEBCA (117 km), because it is the smaller of the two values
